title: Priority Gardener — lightweight request prioritization lanes (brain dump)
text:
Context / problem statement:
- We get a lot of mixed-priority traffic on the hosted API: interactive chat, background embedding jobs, bulk rerank, and internal test harnesses. Today routing is coarse (model + region + token budget) and when capacity is constrained clients experience noisy latency and cost spikes.
- Need a lightweight on-ramp that lets product teams declare per-request intent (fast / normal / cheap / background) and ensure reasonable SLOs without huge infra changes.

Goal:
- Provide a simple 'priority lane' surface that (a) preserves interactive latencies for high intent requests, (b) opportunistically runs cheap variants for low-cost lanes, and (c) makes tradeoffs visible to clients via headers and metrics.
- Keep initial runtime footprint small (policy layer + tagging + queueing/burst token bucket) rather than full-blown scheduling.

Non-goals (MVP):
- Not a replacement for dedicated capacity or long-term tenant-level QoS.
- Not supporting per-customer guaranteed throughput in MVP.

Hypotheses to validate:
- Small number of lanes (3) captures >90% of customer intent patterns with minimal friction.
- Default lane assignment (no client tag) should map to 'normal' and be safe for backward compatibility.
- Exposing basic telemetry (latency p95 by lane, lane drop/retry counts, cost delta) will reduce support tickets and allow clients to optimize usage.

User stories / acceptance criteria:
- As an app developer I can set lane=fast|normal|cheap in request metadata and get back a response header X-Redwood-Lane that confirms assignment. (AC: header appears, p95 latency for fast lane < 200ms for 2k tokens under nominal load)
- As SRE I can see per-lane capacity utilization and configure lane weights for short timespans. (AC: Console shows lane charts, ability to change fast:normal:cheap weights for a region)
- As product I can run an A/B where 10% of traffic gets routed to 'cheap' mode that uses a quantized variant and measure delta in cost and quality. (AC: experiment telemetry, rollback button)

High level design (MVP):
- Client opt-in tag or header: X-Redwood-Lane: fast|normal|cheap. Default=normal.
- Policy layer (edge): reads lane + model + customer tier -> assignment to policy outcome: direct-run, queued-with-burst, fallback-variant.
- Lightweight local queue per worker group with two token buckets: guaranteed burst tokens for fast lane and shared pool for normal/cheap.
- Cheap lane -> prefer quantized model variant or lower temperature/shorter max_tokens heuristic. Fast lane -> pin to high-fidelity model instance when available.
- Telemetry: lane tag persisted in trace, metrics (p50/p95/p99, tokens, cost-estimate), and synthetic checks per lane.

Experiment matrix (first 6 weeks):
1) Shadow lanes: accept header but don't alter routing; collect p95/p99 and cost delta.
2) Burst-buckets: enable small burst tokens for fast lane under load; measure tail latency reductions.
3) Cheap-variant A/B: 10/90 split, quantized model for cheap lane; evaluate regeneration rate and quality metrics.
4) Auto-fallback: policy to switch cheap->normal when quality regression > threshold.

Open questions / risks:
- How to estimate "cost delta" per-request pre-execution? (rough proxy = token_count * model_cost_rate)
- Client misuse: users might mark everything as "fast"; need server-side enforcement (tier limits) and visibility.
- Fairness across customers at peak — need to align with overall routing/fallback policies.

Metrics to track (MVP):
- Adoption: fraction of requests with lane header by customer cohort.
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 by lane, and tail improvement vs baseline.
- Cost: per-token estimated unit cost by lane; delta for cheap variant.
- Quality: regenerate rate, eval-on-sample score drop for cheap lane.
- Support signals: number of tickets referencing lane behavior.

Rollout plan (sketch):
- Week 0-1: spec + simple header acceptance + telemetry shadow (no behavior change).
- Week 2-3: burst-token behavior for fast lane in a single region, rollout to 10% traffic.
- Week 4: cheap-variant A/B for internal beta customers.
- Week 5-6: open beta with console controls for lane weights and experiment toggles.

Engineering notes / tasks:
- Edge: header parser, policy evaluation hook, ensure idempotency for retries.
- Serving runtime: lightweight variant switcher (quantized model variant registry).
- Console: lane dashboards (utilization, p95), toggle for region-level lane weights.
- Billing: ensure lane tags flow into cost estimates and billing metadata.
- Tests: synthetic load tests per lane, chaos tests for queue saturation.

Quick UX sketches (for Console):
- Per-route card: toggle lanes on/off, set default lane, set region weights, view p95 by lane.
- Experiment panel: create A/B with percentage, assign cheap variant, auto-rollback slider.

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Draft small API proposal for header + SDK helper (Python/Node examples).
- Spike telemetry schema and add synthetic check for 99th percentile per lane.
- Sync with SRE about guardrails for client-provided lane tags.

Notes to self:
- Keep language simple for customers: "lanes" not "QoS classes".
- Watch for telemetry cardinality explosion if we tag too many dimensions.
- Prioritize minimal surface area that can be iterated quickly.

Random ideas to revisit later:
- Allow contextual lane boxing: a long-running conversation can be tagged as "cheap" for background summarization jobs only.
- Per-customer lane credits (pre-purchased fast tokens).
- Automatic lane suggestion model: infer user intent from prompt and suggest lane in SDK.

End.
